question: What is the SI unit of radioactivity?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Becquerel**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **SI unit of radioactivity** is the **Becquerel (Bq)**.
 
• It measures the rate of radioactive decay, defined as one disintegration (decay) per second.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Faraday**:
 
• Named after Michael Faraday, the Faraday is a unit associated with electric charge, not radioactivity. Specifically, it refers to the charge of one mole of electrons (approximately 96,485 coulombs) and is often used in electrochemistry.
 
• **Rutherford**:
 
• The Rutherford (Rd) is an older, non-SI unit of radioactivity. It was defined as **1 million disintegrations per second** but has largely been replaced by the Becquerel in modern scientific contexts.
 
• **Curie (Ci)**:
 
• The **Curie** is another unit of radioactivity, named after Marie Curie, and was historically used before the Becquerel. One Curie equals **3.7 × 10¹⁰ disintegrations per second** (the approximate activity of 1 gram of radium-226).
 
 
• Although still sometimes used, the Curie has mostly been replaced by the Becquerel in the SI system.
